tspan.tspan: Predicting Interstitial ELF and Mapping Void Connectivity for
A graph neural network predicts the electron localization function (ELF) at interstitial voids; a geometric network labels how those voids connect
· Advisor: Justin Andrews · Department of Chemistry, Purdue University · weilana@purdue.edu
Electrons that sit between the atoms
In an electride, some valence electrons are not
bound to any atom. They localize in the empty
space (voids) of the crystal and act as the anions.
Schematic: cations (+) with electrons (e−) held in
Those voids can be isolated or connected, which sets the dimensionality
The electron localization function (ELF) runs from
0 to 1 and measures how localized electrons are
compared with a uniform electron gas (0.5).
An ELF maximum inside a void
ELF needs a DFT calculation for
: predict ELF at each void without DFT, and map how the voids connect. We built two void-centered tools and tested
TOOL 1 · PREDICT ELF AT EACH VOID
Can a graph network predict the ELF at each candidate void from the
Atoms and candidate voids are both nodes of one periodic graph, joined by distance edges.
Message passing gathers each void’s atomic neighborhood and returns one ELF value at the void

tspan.tspan: Predicted vs. DFT ELF on the test set
A void’s own geometry does no better than predicting the mean
(0.139 vs 0.141); adding its atomic neighborhood cuts the error by more than half.
Data: ELFNet [2], 50,000 DFT structures (metal frameworks derived from compressed hydrides), split
TOOL 2 · MAP HOW THE VOIDS CONNECT
Can geometry alone recover the dimensionality reported for electrides?
Each atom blocks a sphere (ionic radius + probe radius). We follow the open space through the
crystal and count how many directions it repeats in: none (0D), one (1D) or two (2D).

g.text: must fit to pass through a neck
The path repeats through every cell

tspan.tspan: 0.4 to 1.8 Å in 0.05 Å steps (29 sizes)
In 91 of 167 electrides labeled 0D, the open space connects at some probe size.
The space forms a path, but the electrons may still sit in separate pockets.
Open space is not the same as electrons
The same open channel can hold connected electrons (1D) or separate pockets (0D); only the ELF at its bottleneck tells them apart.
